raw_case_text:
A 36-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital on March 3, 2020 for more than 1 months of recurrent fever. She was from Hengyang City, Hunan Province, China. Upon admission, she went through a physical examination and was found in poor general conditions. Weight: 46 kg; height: 165 cm, heart rate (HR): 115 beats/min; respiratory rate (RR): 19 breaths/min; blood pressure (BP): 112/70 mmHg; pulse oximetry (SPO2): 97%; temperature:36.6 C; cardiopulmonary auscultation with systolic murmur in mesocardium; blood count with leukocytosis (18,000/mm3) and deviation to the left; neutrophils 63%; Hemoglobin 62 g/L; moderate thrombocytopenia (platelets: 82,000/mm3), high C reactive protein (61 mg/L).
The patient was diagnosed with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) 6 years ago. She had no other disease history. In the past 6 years, the patient had regular hemodialysis twice a week via a right internal carotid artery catheter. On January 25, 2020, the patient began to have fever with the highest temperature of 39.6 C. There was no cough, sputum, rash and joint pain. The patient visited the local county people's Hospital, and the chest Computed Tomography (CT) results showed that the patient had pulmonary infection (Multiple nodules in the lower lobe of the right lung). The COVID-19 throat swabs PCR result and antibody result were both negative. Blood culture results of paired blood samples taken from bilateral arms prior to the empirical use of antibiotics were also negative. Due to the long-term use of catheter dialysis, the local hospital doctors considered that the fever might be caused by bacterial catheter infection. Therefore, the patient was given intravenous meropenem 500 mg 12 hourly and vancomycin 750 mg 24 hourly for empirical anti-infection treatment. However, the treatment effect was not good, and the patient still had fever. After 3 days of hospitalization, the doctor pulled out the patient's dialysis catheter and changed to direct puncture dialysis. The results of microbial culture on the tip of the removed catheter were also negative. After the removal of the catheter, the patient's condition was still not improved and still had fever, so she was transferred to our hospital to continue treatment. The venous blood samples of the patient was sent for PACEseq metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) (Hugobiotech, Beijing, China) on a Nextseq550 platform (Illumina), with results indicating A. flavus infection. So we adjusted the treatment to voriconazole 400 mg 12 hourly for 2 doses then 200 mg every 12 h (target trough concentration of 1.5-4.0 mug ml-1) and moxifloxacin 400 mg 24 hourly for anti-infection treatment, and the patient's fever symptoms were finally controlled.
The patient's Color Doppler ultrasound and superior vena cava Computed Tomography Angiography (CTA) examination showed tricuspid valve vegetation, moderate tricuspid insufficiency, scattered infection in both lungs, thrombosis in right internal jugular vein and superior vena cava, and chronic embolism of right pulmonary artery (Figure 1). Transesophageal echocardiography showed that the atrium of the anterior tricuspid valve had multiple moderate echo masses, which were about 17 x 15 mm above the apex and 18 x 10 mm near the valve root, and swayed back and forth with the opening and closing of the leaflets. Some of the masses seemed to be connected with the septal valve tip. A few masses attached to the apex of the tricuspid valve were slightly detached into the coronary sinus orifice with the leaflet when the valve was closed (Figure 2).
On March 30, 2020, the patient underwent tricuspid valve removal, tricuspid valve replacement, and superior vena cava right atrium thrombectomy under general anesthesia and cardiopulmonary bypass. Histopathological examination of tricuspid valve vegetations revealed mixed bacterial thrombus in tricuspid valve with granulation tissue hyperplasia (Figure 3). Results of tissue samples sent for PACEseq mNGS confirmation (Hugobiotech, Beijing, China) and subsequent vegetative culture results from Sabouraud medium and BACT/ALERT (bioMerieux) all confirmed the presence of A. flavus.
Due to the improved clinical results, the patient was discharged from hospital 1 week after sugery with treatment on voriconazole 0.2 g twice a day and after following up about a year later, there were no complications or adverse events (the intuitive treatment process can be seen in Figure 4).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 36-year-old woman on chronic catheter-based hemodialysis presented with a >1-month history of recurrent high fevers up to 39.6 C unresponsive to broad-spectrum antibiotics and catheter removal.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Maintained on twice-weekly hemodialysis via a right internal carotid/jugular catheter for 6 years, the patient developed recurrent high fevers (up to 39.6 C) starting January 25, 2020 without cough, rash, or arthralgias. At a local hospital, chest CT showed multiple right lower lobe nodules; despite empirical IV meropenem (500 mg q12h), vancomycin (750 mg q24h), and removal of the dialysis catheter on day 3, her high fevers persisted, prompting transfer to our hospital on March 3, 2020.
subjective.past_medical_history: End-stage renal disease (ESRD) diagnosed 6 years prior, maintained on twice-weekly hemodialysis via a long-term right cervical vascular catheter.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for >1 month of recurrent high fevers; negative for cough, sputum, skin rash, or joint pain.

objective.physical_examination: Poor general condition; weight 46 kg, height 165 cm, heart rate 115 bpm, respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, SpO2 97%, and temperature 36.6 C (spiking to 39.6 C during febrile episodes). Cardiac auscultation revealed a mesocardial systolic murmur.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed leukocytosis (WBC 18,000/mm3 with left shift, 63% neutrophils), severe anemia (hemoglobin 62 g/L), moderate thrombocytopenia (platelets 82,000/mm3), and elevated CRP (61 mg/L). Paired peripheral blood cultures, removed dialysis catheter tip culture, and SARS-CoV-2 throat swab PCR and antibody tests were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Peripheral blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (PACEseq mNGS on Illumina NextSeq 550) detected Aspergillus flavus. Color Doppler ultrasound, superior vena cava CT angiography (CTA), and transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) demonstrated multiple large mobile tricuspid valve vegetations (17 x 15 mm and 18 x 10 mm on the anterior/septal leaflets prolapsing into the coronary sinus orifice) with moderate tricuspid regurgitation, thrombosis of the right internal jugular vein and superior vena cava, chronic right pulmonary artery embolism, and scattered bilateral pulmonary septic nodules. Following open-heart tricuspid valve replacement and SVC/right atrial thrombectomy on March 30, 2020, valve vegetation histopathology, tissue PACEseq mNGS, and cultures on Sabouraud medium and BacT/ALERT all confirmed Aspergillus flavus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Dialysis-catheter-associated native tricuspid valve Aspergillus flavus infective endocarditis complicated by right internal jugular vein and superior vena cava thrombosis and septic right pulmonary artery embolism, rapidly diagnosed by peripheral blood mNGS despite negative conventional blood and catheter-tip cultures and definitively confirmed by excised valve vegetation histopathology, tissue mNGS, and fungal culture. Treated with TDM-guided voriconazole (400 mg q12h loading for 2 doses, then 200 mg q12h targeting troughs of 1.5-4.0 ug/mL) plus moxifloxacin (400 mg daily) which controlled the fever, followed by surgical tricuspid valve replacement and SVC/right atrial thrombectomy on March 30, 2020 and outpatient oral voriconazole (200 mg twice daily), remaining complication-free at 1-year follow-up.
